text: U.S. effort to replicate China’s Belt and Road Initiative energy infrastructure investments abroad would likely require billions of U.S. dollars in aid and decades for implementation. As of 2025, China’s Belt and Road Initiative is estimated to have a total cost of $1.308 trillion since 2013 for construction and investments across 150 countries, with $40 billion in 2024 and $44 billion in the first half of 2025 on energy engagement (representing 35% of China’s international efforts in 2025) (Nedopil 2025). The G7-led Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment (PGII) announced in 2022 was designed to finance $600 billion in infrastructure, including energy infrastructure, for low- to middle-income countries by 2027 (Brownstein 2023) as an effort to build global influence in response to China’s efforts (Losos and Fetter 2022). In addition, a western supply chain of energy assets would be necessary to reduce the risk of Chinese influence and control of software or hardware (Sutherland and Sutter 2024). Figure C-1. Image by NLR C.2 Local Energy Vulnerabilities Key East Asian allies, such as South Korea and Japan, have high energy consumption rates and a significant reliance on imported hydrocarbons (ITA 2021). The Philippines relies on imported fossil fuels for more than half its consumption (Prétat et al. 2024), leaving the country vulnerable to supply disruptions. This dependence has acted as a catalyst for the accelerated adoption of advanced energy technologies by these countries, with Japan investing ¥15 trillion ($107.5 billion) in their hydrogen infrastructure and launching multiple large-scale battery energy storage systems, including a 69.6-MWh sodium-sulfur project (Ravichandran 2023). South Korea, which holds more than 30% of the Asia-Pacific’s battery energy storage system market, aims to reach 63 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 25 gigawatts (GW)/127 GWh in storage capacity by 2036, while the Philippines is developing one of the world’s largest battery energy storage system portfolios, at 1,000 MW, and has secured more than $13 billion in foreign investment for advanced energy technology and storage projects (Ravichandran 2023). But even as these countries adopt advanced energy technologies, their strategies introduce new forms of dependence. More than 85% of battery energy storage systems expected to come online globally in 2024 will use lithium-iron-phosphate chemistries, for which China controls nearly the entire supply chain—including raw material processing and cell manufacturing (Hughes 2025). As a result, more than 75% of global battery deployments outside China still rely on Chinese supply chains (Hughes 2025), underscoring that energy security challenges persist. Such reliance on Chinese-sourced battery components could introduce additional cyber risks to the energy infrastructure of host nations and (by extension) to the U.S. installations operating within those countries. China’s dominance of several aspects of the advanced energy technology market has left island nations increasingly dependent on China for these technologies and for supporting grid infrastructure upgrades.
